newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Commodities the key to bold Australia rail plan.
newsitem.headline: Commodities the key to bold Australia rail plan.

text.p: A A$10 billion proposal to build a 4,000 kilometre railway from Melbourne through Australia's east-side commodities belt to the Top End port city of Darwin has obtained in-principle backing of international financiers, the venture's chief promoter told Reuters.
The proposed rail link, which would carry 10 times the freight of the A$1.0 billion, 1,410 km line proposed for Alice Springs to Darwin, would revolutionise the export trade, its promoters said.
Many big international groups had expressed interest in financing the project or joining the consortium, Everald Compton, the project's main promoter, told Reuters.
Australian Prime Minister John Howard encouraged Compton in April to proceed with feasibility studies, he also said.
Compton's group, Australian Transport and Energy Corridor Pty Ltd (ATEC), was formed last week to proceed with feasibility studies into the venture.

Other members of the ATEC group include former Labor Senator Stephen Loosley, former Liberal Party president John Valder, Tim Fairfax, of the Fairfax media family and Charles Blunt, American Chamber of Commerce in Australia executive director.
Leading accounting firm KPMG now has been commissioned to assess the railway's revenue potential.
A KPMG official told Reuters on Tuesday that work was just beginning but that an inquiry had been received from Japan that morning.
Informal discussions had been held with financiers in New York and London, as well as with large-scale potential members of the plan's consortium.
These included an international railway construction group, Compton said.
He would not name names but said large groups from the U.S., Britain, France, Italy, Russia and Japan had expressed interest.
"We don't see it as a problem to get the A$10 billion capital. Financiers in New York and London don't see a problem getting the money if it's the right financial deal," he said.
"The biggest issue in this is to get five governments to agree to co-operate," he said.
The railway would require agreement from the Australian government, from governments of the states of Victoria, New South Wales (NSW) and Queensland, as well as from the Northern Territory (NT).
Negotiations with governments had begun, Compton said.
"We believe we can do it and we're not playing games. We've put up our own capital to get this thing going and we believe we're going to build it," he said.

The proposed Melbourne-Darwin link would travel through the Goulburn Valley dairy area, fruit producing areas near the NSW-Victoria border, the Riverina wheat area, the great western wheat plains in western NSW, the Darling Downs cotton and grains region, the Queensland coal fields, the Mount Isa base metal region in Queensland's west, then on through the NT's Tennant Creek gold province.
The plan envisages high-speed 200-300 km-an-hour trains transporting commodities in 24 hours for export through Darwin, Australia's closest port city to Asia and other world markets.
Compton sees industry establishing along the rail link.
"It will simply revolutionise the country and I'm not romancing. This thing is going to happen, its time has come and we're going to make it happen, as simple as that," Compton said.
Compton is an international fundraising consultant and former head of Compton International, which he sold a year ago.
